topic.name: Phase Portraits for Linear Systems With Zero Eigenvalues

question.text:
\[ \begin{cases} x'(t) = x(t)-y(t) \\[5pt] y'(t) = -x(t)+y(t) \end{cases} \] Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are $\lambda_1=0$ and $\lambda_2=2,$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are $\mathbf{v}_1 = [1, \ 1]^T$ and $\mathbf{v}_2 = [-1, \ 1]^T,$ respectively. Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the system?

Hint: Here, the dotted line represents the equilibrium solutions.
question.explanation:
The general solution of the system is \[ \mathbf{x}(t)= \begin{bmatrix} x(t)\\y(t)\end{bmatrix} = c_1 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + c_2 e^{2t} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Let's now sketch the phase portrait.

  • First, notice that $\mathbf{x}_E(t) = c_1 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$ are the equilibrium solutions of the system since $\mathbf{x}'_E(t) = \mathbf{0}.$ These solutions form the line with the equation $y=x$ in the phase space, as shown below.
  • Now, the line that passes through the origin and is parallel to $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$ has the equation $ y= -x $ and the straight-line solutions of the form $ c_2 e^{2t} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} $ lie on that line. Since $e^{2t} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t \to \infty.$

All other non-equilibrium solutions are parallel to the vector $\mathbf{v}_2.$ So, the phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

question.text:

The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are $\lambda_1=0$ and $\lambda_2=-4,$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are $\mathbf{v}_1 = [2, \ 1]^T$ and $\mathbf{v}_2 = [-2, \ 1]^T,$ respectively. Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the system?

Hint: Here, the dotted line represents the equilibrium solutions.
question.explanation:
The general solution of the system is \[ \mathbf{x}(t)= \begin{bmatrix} x(t)\\y(t)\end{bmatrix} = c_1 \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + c_2 e^{-4t} \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Let's now sketch the phase portrait.

  • First, notice that $\mathbf{x}_E(t) = c_1 \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$ are the equilibrium solutions of the system since $\mathbf{x}'_E(t) = \mathbf{0}.$ These solutions form the line with the equation $y=\dfrac12x$ in the phase space, as shown below.
  • Now, the line that passes through the origin and is parallel to $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$ has the equation $ y= -\dfrac12x $ and the straight-line solutions of the form $ c_2 e^{-4t} \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} $ lie on that line. Since $e^{-4t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t \to \infty.$

All other non-equilibrium solutions are parallel to the vector $\mathbf{v}_2.$ So, the phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

example.title: Identifying the Phase Portrait of a System With One Zero Eigenvalue

question.text:
\[ \begin{cases} x'(t) = x(t)-2y(t) \\[5pt] y'(t) = \dfrac{1}{2}x(t)-y(t) \end{cases} \] Consider the system of linear differential equations above. The eigenvector corresponding to the only eigenvalue $\lambda=0$ of the system's matrix $A$ is $\mathbf{v} = [2, \ 1]^T.$ The vector $\mathbf{w} = [2, \ 0]^T$ is such that $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$ Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the system?

Hint: Here, the dotted line represents the equilibrium solutions.
question.explanation:
Since we have a repeated eigenvalue $\lambda=0$ (of multiplicity two) and only one corresponding eigenvector $\mathbf{v},$ the solution of the system is given by \[ \mathbf{x}(t) = c_1\mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t} + c_2 (\mathbf{v} te^{\lambda t} + \mathbf{w}e^{\lambda t} \, ), \] where $\mathbf{w}$ is a solution to the equation $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf{w}= \mathbf{v}.$

In our case, \[ \lambda = 0, \qquad \mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{w} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}. \] Thus, the general solution of the system is \begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} x(t)\\y(t)\end{bmatrix} &= c_1 \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + c_2 \left( \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} t + \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \right) \\[5pt] &= c_1 \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + c_2 \begin{bmatrix} 2t+2 \\ t \end{bmatrix}, \qquad c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}. \end{align*}

First, notice that $\mathbf{x}_E(t) = c_1 \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$ are equilibrium solutions of the system since $\mathbf{x}'_E(t) = \mathbf{0}.$ These solutions form the line with the equation $y=\dfrac{1}{2}x$ in the phase space, as shown below.

Now, we consider some general solutions of the form \[ \begin{bmatrix} x(t)\\y(t)\end{bmatrix} = c_1 \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} + c_2 \begin{bmatrix} 2t+2 \\ t \end{bmatrix}. \] For example:

  • When $c_1=1$ and $c_2=1,$ we get the following curve: \[ \begin{cases} x = 2t+4 \\[3pt] y = t+1 \end{cases} \] Let's add it to the phase space:
  • When $c_1=-1$ and $c_2=-1,$ we get the following curve: \[ \begin{cases} x = -2t-4 \\[3pt] y = -t-1 \end{cases} \] Let's add it to the phase space:

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:
